steelman: A single scalar merge rate is a biased and noisy estimator of an agent's code quality, because the merge/reject event is produced by a human review process, not by the code alone. Two independent empirical legs support this. First (s1, 11,048 mixed-agent PRs), rejection is mostly not a quality verdict: only 35.7% of rejected agentic PRs reflect clear agentic failure, 31.2% are workflow-driven, and 33.1% carry no observable rationale. Second (s2, 567 Claude Code PRs), acceptance is not a clean-pass signal: 83.8% are eventually merged but only 54.9% land without further modification, so roughly a third of merged PRs still needed rework. The discriminating quality signal (rework rate, number of feedback rounds, reviewer commits, decision rationale) lives in the reviewer-interaction trace, which outcome-only metrics throw away. Therefore a cross-agent leaderboard built purely on the merge label partly measures the repos and their review processes rather than the agents.
strongest_attack: The hardest attack is a sharpened apples-to-oranges plus inference-gap objection. Granting that merge outcomes carry workflow noise, that noise only corrupts a cross-AGENT ranking if it is CORRELATED with agent identity. The s1 rejection decomposition is measured across mixed agentic tools pooled together and says nothing about per-agent variation; s2 is a different dataset, different authors, Claude Code only. Neither study demonstrates that workflow noise differs systematically by agent. If every repo reviews all agents by roughly the same house rules, then workflow variance is random error that inflates the variance of the merge rate but leaves the expected ordering intact: a noisy but unbiased ranking still ranks agents, not repos. On that reading the prescriptive claim c4 (leaderboards rank repos, not agents) overreaches from the evidence actually presented, and what remains (a merge is a social decision, and merge rate blends clean and reworked passes) risks collapsing into something a careful reader already concedes.
reconciliation: The thesis survives, because the missing correlation condition is in fact satisfied by how agentic-PR leaderboards are built, and the thesis hedges with the word partly rather than claiming total corruption. Scraped cross-agent leaderboards do not hold the repo and review process fixed: each agent is scored across whatever repositories it happened to be deployed in, which is exactly the s1-versus-s2 situation generalized. When agents are ranked over NON-identical repo populations, workflow variance is confounded with agent identity by construction, so it becomes bias in the ordering, not merely error variance. The attack's escape hatch (same repos review all agents identically) is not how these leaderboards are actually assembled, so it does not hold. The two studies are not averaged into one convergent number; they are two logically independent legs, each valid within its own population (rejections are mostly not quality-driven; merges are mostly not clean), and the thesis explicitly acknowledges the population difference rather than hiding it. The 83.8% figure is not self-undermining either: it is cited to be discounted, and its 54.9% clean-pass decomposition is itself part of the interaction trace the thesis is promoting.
strengthened_argument: State the confound condition explicitly. Merge-rate leaderboards mislead specifically because agents are compared across different repo populations, so review-process variance is confounded with agent identity rather than averaging out; this is the general form of the s1-versus-s2 mismatch, not an accident of two papers. The evidence establishes the mechanism on each side independently: rejection is mostly workflow or unexplained, not clear failure (35.7% clear-failure share, s1), and acceptance hides rework (only 54.9% of merges clean, s2). The remedy is to hold the repo fixed or to score the reviewer-interaction trace (rework rate, feedback rounds, reviewer commits, rationale), which is closer to a per-PR quality measurement and far less hostage to which repo did the reviewing. Claim only what follows: the merge label is a workflow-contaminated proxy whose cross-agent ordering is unreliable whenever populations differ, and the interaction trace is the more discriminating signal, without asserting that the trace is perfectly clean or that merge rate carries zero information.
reason: The core claim is non-trivial (named leaderboards do treat merge rate as the headline agent-quality score), falsifiable, and backed by two independent quantified legs; the strongest attack (workflow noise may be uncorrelated with agent, so merge rate could still rank unbiasedly) is defeated because real cross-agent leaderboards score agents over non-identical repo populations, which makes the confound a bias in the ordering, so the hedged thesis holds in its strengthened form.
